summary: one file's one composition
doc:
A piece is one composition: everything a single file says about one work — its title, its starting tempo, meter, and key, its score, and its studio. Every `.musa` file that is not a `library` holds exactly one.

```musa
piece "Ruchenitsa" { meter 7/8; score { … } }
```

summary: how fast, written where it changes
the count, written where it changes
doc:
A meter statement is the count the music is measured in, as a fraction of the whole note: `meter 7/8;` counts seven eighths to a bar. It changes mid-piece by being written again where it changes, and `meter none;` stops the barlines entirely until the next one.

```musa
meter 4/4;
```

summary: the key signature, written where it changes
doc:
A key statement names the key the music is in — a pitch class and a mode. It is notation and knowledge, not a transposition: the notes are written at their sounding pitch either way.

```musa
key a minor;
```

summary: a second line under the title
doc:
A subtitle is a line of front matter printed under the piece's title — a dedication, a movement name, an opus number.

```musa
subtitle "for eight players";
```

summary: who wrote it
doc:
The composer line names who wrote the piece, printed in the front matter.

```musa
composer "J. S. Bach";
```

summary: who arranged it
doc:
The arranger line names who arranged the piece, printed in the front matter beside the composer.

```musa
arranger "F. Busoni";
```

summary: the rights line
doc:
The copyright line is the rights notice printed in the front matter.

```musa
copyright "© 2026 J. Reinhold";
```

summary: a named musical idea, used by name
doc:
A motif is a musical idea said once and given a name: a phrase, a figure, a rhythm, with parameters for what changes between uses. Write it out where it is wanted with `use name(args);` — an edit to the motif then reaches every occurrence.

```musa
motif sigh(root: Pitch) { root/8 root/8 }
```

summary: the parts and their music
doc:
The score block is the music itself: the parts, each with its clef and its voices, written in the order they read. Everything before it is the header; everything after it is the studio.

```musa
score { part violin { clef treble; voice one { … } } }
```

summary: one instrument's staff
doc:
A part is one instrument's lane through the piece: its own clef, its own voices, and — when it differs from the piece — its own meter or tempo (polymeter, polytempo). A part is notation, not sound; the studio decides what plays it.

```musa
part kaval { clef treble; meter 7/8; voice melody { … } }
```

summary: one rhythmic line inside a part
doc:
A voice is one line of rhythm inside a part: notes, rests, and everything written where the music reaches it. Two voices in one part share the staff and count their own bars independently.

```musa
voice right { c4/4 d4/4 }
```

summary: which clef the staff reads
doc:
A clef statement says which clef a part reads from here — `treble`, `bass`, `alto`, `tenor`. Written in a voice, it changes mid-part where the music reaches it.

```musa
clef treble;
```

summary: write out a motif where it stands
doc:
`use` writes out a declared motif where it stands, with arguments for its parameters: `use sigh(e5);` is the motif spelled here, once. It is a splice and not a call: the music arrives at the cursor and is sequenced there. Bringing in another file is `import`, which is a different statement and now a different word.

```musa
use sigh(e5);
```

summary: bring another file's names into this one
doc:
`import` reads a relative library file or a bundled module and binds its declarations as if they were written here: `import "../library/motifs.musa";` or `import std::core;`. Add `as name` to bring it in under a different name. Bundled modules are ordinary Musa source and add no hidden prelude.

```musa
import std::core;
```

summary: the region a package reads, and the import that names its reader
the same music, moved in pitch
doc:
Transpose plays music moved by a written interval such as `P5` or `M3`; the block and function forms have the same musical meaning. Supplying only the interval makes a reusable answer function.

```musa
let answer: Music -> Music = transpose(P5);
```

summary: the direction of a transposition, downward
doc:
`down` marks a transposition as downward: `transpose down P5 { … }` lowers its contents a perfect fifth. Its counterpart is `up`.

```musa
transpose down m2 { … }
```

summary: the direction of a transposition, upward
doc:
`up` marks a transposition as upward: `transpose up P5 { … }` raises its contents a perfect fifth. Its counterpart is `down`.

```musa
transpose up M3 { … }
```

summary: silence with a duration
doc:
A rest is notated silence: it fills its duration in the bar exactly like a note fills its own. A bar that does not add up — rests included — is an error, because a missing rest is a missing beat.

```musa
rest/4
```

summary: repeat music, or make a finite list
one measure, named
doc:
A bar is one measure of music: what a player reads between two barlines, and the unit that must add up to the meter. Write it with `|`, the way notation draws it. The keyword is for the bar that earns a name — `bar head { … }` — which makes it an address an edit or a reader can point at.

```musa
bar head { c4/4 d4/4 e4/4 f4/4 }
```

summary: a claim the compiler proves
doc:
An assertion states something objective about the music inside it and makes the compiler check it: `assert pitches_in(scale c major) { … }` says every note sounded there is spelled in C major, and a note that is not stops the compilation with the note named. It changes nothing — a claim that holds returns exactly what was written — and it is per-passage, never a rule about the piece.

The claims are `fills_meter()`, `pitches_in(scale)`, `realizes(chord, policy)`, `voices(count)`, and `within_ranges(ranges)`.

```musa
assert voices(4) { [c3 g3 e4 c5]/1 }
```

summary: an unmeasured stretch with a scope
doc:
A senza block is unmeasured music with braces around it: the barlines stop for exactly its contents and the meter returns after, without the `meter none;` … `meter 4/4;` pair you could otherwise forget the second half of. Cadenzas and chant are written this way.

```musa
senza { c4/1 g4/1 }
```

summary: what changes on a given pass of a repeat
doc:
An ending block plays only on the numbered pass of the enclosing `repeat`: `ending 1 { … }` the first time, `ending 2 { … }` the second. It is how a repeated strain gets a different close.

```musa
repeat 2 { use strain(); ending 1 { c4/1 } ending 2 { g4/1 } }
```

summary: a labeled block a mobile can arrange
doc:
A fragment is a named block of music that means nothing in source order: it becomes music when a `mobile` arranges it among others. Fragments are how musa writes music whose order is chosen, not fixed.

```musa
fragment a { c4/4 d4/4 }
```

summary: fragments in a chosen order
doc:
A mobile block plays its fragments in an order the performance chooses: `mobile { a; b; c; }` is those fragments, balanced like the sculpture, not fixed like a score. Each performance records the order it picked, so the chosen form is a fact you can read.

```musa
mobile { a; b; a; c; }
```

summary: a constrained improvisation
doc:
An improvise statement asks for an improvisation over a span and a harmony: `improvise 8/1 over "Dm7 | G7";`. The constraints are written; the notes are the performance's, and the seed decides which ones.

```musa
improvise 4/1 over "Cmaj7";
```

summary: how far a gradual change reaches
doc:
`over` says how far a gradual change reaches, in the change's own unit: `tempo 1/4 = 72 to 48 over 2/1;` takes two whole notes to get there. It can also follow a worded marking — `tempo "rit." over 1/1;` — where the player owns the speed.

```musa
tempo "poco rit." over 1/1;
```

summary: a phrase mark over the block
doc:
A slur block is played legato under one bow or breath: the notation curve over its contents. It changes how the notes connect, not which notes they are.

```musa
slur { c4/8 d4/8 e4/8 }
```

summary: a loudness marking
doc:
A dynamic statement is a loudness marking — `pp` through `fff` — written where it takes force. It is a mark on the page, not a decibel value; what it does to the notes is the performance layer's business.

```musa
dynamic mf;
```

summary: notes in the time of fewer
doc:
A tuplet block fits its contents into the time a different count would take: `tuplet 3/2 { … }` is three in the time of two. The ratio is exact — tuplets are arithmetic, not feel.

```musa
tuplet 3/2 { c4/8 d4/8 e4/8 }
```

summary: rules for how the written becomes the played
doc:
A performance block declares how notation becomes playing: `mark`, `dynamic`, `groove`, and `grace` rules that say what a marking does to time and loudness. It is the piece's own answer to "what does this mark mean here", kept separate from the notation it interprets.

```musa
performance { mark accent { weight: 1.3; } }
```

summary: which performance profile realizes this part
doc:
A profile statement names the performance profile a part is played with — a named bundle of humanization settings declared in a `performance` block. Without one, the part is played as written.

```musa
profile strings;
```

summary: a performance mark: accent, fermata, rehearsal letter, sample
a named timing feel
doc:
A groove statement applies a named timing feel — a swing or shuffle declared in the `performance` block — to the music from here. The name is notation; the rule is what it does to the beats.

```musa
groove shuffle;
```

summary: notes crushed before the beat
doc:
A grace block holds grace notes: small notes that lean on the event after them and fill no time in the bar. Where they steal their time from is the `performance` block's `grace` rule.

```musa
grace { d5 } c5/4
```

summary: what plays the score
doc:
The studio block is everything after the music: the patches that make sound, the assignments of parts to them, the buses, sends, routes, and modulations that wire the mix. The score says what the notes are; the studio says what they sound like.

```musa
studio { patch pad { … } assign violin -> pad; }
```

summary: a signal graph with a name
doc:
A patch is a named signal chain: oscillators, filters, envelopes, and effects wired with `|>` into one instrument. A part is realized by the patch an `assign` points at it — and a patch nothing assigns is wired to silence.

```musa
patch glass_pad { oscillator(sine) |> lowpass(cutoff: 1400 Hz) |> output; }
```

summary: let a signal drive a parameter
doc:
A modulate statement wires a control signal into a patch parameter: `modulate lfo -> glass_pad.lowpass.cutoff;` lets the LFO move the filter. The path names patch, node, and parameter with dots.

```musa
modulate lfo -> pad.lowpass.cutoff;
```

summary: a shared channel in the mix
doc:
A bus is a named channel signals can be sent to and mixed through — a reverb hall every part shares. Parts reach it with `send`; it reaches the output with `route`.

```musa
bus hall { reverb(room: 0.8); }
```

summary: which patch realizes a part
doc:
An assign statement points a part at a patch: `assign violin -> glass_pad;` says the violin's notes are played by that graph. A part without one keeps the default instrument.

```musa
assign reeds -> reed;
```

summary: where a signal goes in the mix
doc:
A route statement sends a part's or bus's output to a destination: `route violin -> master;`. Without one, a part still reaches the master; a route is for when it should go somewhere else, or somewhere else too.

```musa
route hall -> master;
```

summary: tap some of a signal into a bus
doc:
A send statement taps a level of a part's or bus's signal into a bus: `send violin -> hall at -18 dB;` puts some of the violin in the hall while it also plays dry. The level is written with `at`.

```musa
send strings -> hall at -14 dB;
```

summary: the final mix bus
doc:
`master` is the mix's final destination: the bus everything audible ultimately routes to. Route to it explicitly when a signal should arrive from more than one path.

```musa
route hall -> master;
```

summary: the level of a send
doc:
`at` writes the level of a `send`: `send violin -> hall at -18 dB;` is how much of the violin the hall gets, in decibels.

```musa
send drums -> room at -24 dB;
```

summary: where a patch's signal leaves
doc:
`output` ends a patch's signal chain: whatever reaches it is the sound the patch makes. A chain without one builds to nothing, and the compiler says so.

```musa
oscillator(sine) |> gain(-15 dB) |> output;
```

summary: the standard library's pitch module
the same music, at a different speed ratio
doc:
Stretch plays music scaled in written time by an exact factor: `stretch 3/2 { … }` takes half again as long. `stretch(3/2)` is the reusable function form with the same meaning.

```musa
let broaden: Music -> Music = stretch(3/2);
```

summary: the block, backwards
doc:
Retrograde plays its music backwards — the last event first. The block and `retrograde(subject)` function forms are the same classical transformation.

```musa
let answer: Music = retrograde(subject);
```

summary: the block, mirrored in pitch
doc:
Invert mirrors music around an axis pitch: what went up goes down by the same written interval. `invert(c5)` makes a reusable function; the block writes the axis with `around`.

```musa
let mirror: Music -> Music = invert(c5);
```

summary: the axis of an inversion
doc:
`around` names the axis pitch an `invert` block mirrors about: `invert around c5 { … }` leaves `c5` where it is and flips everything else across it.

```musa
invert around g4 { … }
```

summary: respell one note of a motif occurrence
doc:
A `with` clause overrides one parameter of a `use` for this occurrence only: `use sigh() with (root: e5)` is the motif, except here. The definition is untouched.

```musa
use sigh() with (root: e5);
```

summary: a literal note inside an override
doc:
`note` introduces a literal note where an override needs one — the spelled-out exception inside a `with` clause.

```musa
use theme() with (pickup: note c5/8);
```

summary: a named musical sentence
doc:
A phrase block names a stretch of music as one sentence: `phrase "A" { … }`. The name prints and anchors, so editors and readers can talk about the phrase as a thing.

```musa
phrase "question" { use ask(); }
```

summary: a form marker in the score
doc:
A section statement marks a point of form — `section "B";` — anchored to the time it is written at, whether or not a note starts there. It prints and navigates; it changes no note.

```musa
section "Trio";
```

summary: the chord-symbol lane
doc:
A harmony block declares the piece's chord-symbol lane: symbols written at the times they govern, like `harmony { "Dm7" 1/1 "G7" 1/1 }`. The symbols are parsed, so later tooling reads structure instead of letters.

```musa
harmony { "Cmaj7" 2/1 }
```

summary: declarations other pieces can import
doc:
A library is a file of declarations — motifs, fragments, studio patches — meant to be used by other files rather than played itself. A piece brings one in with `import "path";` and then speaks its names as its own.

```musa
library { motif sigh(root: Pitch) { … } }
```

summary: grow toward a named dynamic
doc:
A crescendo block grows the loudness of its contents toward a named arrival: `crescendo to f { … }`. The destination is part of the spelling, because a hairpin that arrives nowhere is a hairpin that lies.

```musa
crescendo to f { use build(); }
```

summary: fade toward a named dynamic
doc:
A diminuendo block fades the loudness of its contents toward a named arrival: `diminuendo to p { … }`. Like the crescendo, the destination is written, not implied.

```musa
diminuendo to pp { use fall(); }
```

summary: where a change arrives
doc:
`to` names where a change arrives: the dynamic a `crescendo` or `diminuendo` reaches, or the tempo a gradual `tempo` change ends at. Arriving somewhere is one idea, so it is one word.

```musa
tempo 1/4 = 72 to 48 over 2/1;
```

summary: give a typed value a name
doc:
A `let` declaration gives an elaboration value a name. The annotation keeps the musical domain visible at the declaration site.

```musa
let answer: Interval = P5;
```

summary: define a total named function
doc:
A function computes an elaboration value from typed parameters. Musa functions are total: they have no unrestricted recursion or effects.

```musa
fn identity(x: Pitch) -> Pitch { x }
```

summary: a notation-first music value
doc:
A `music` block is an expression whose body reads like an ordinary voice: notes remain self-delimiting and reusable material is written with `use`.

```musa
let call: Music = music { c5/4 d5/4 };
```

summary: a quoted kernel composition expression
a type that may contain one value
doc:
`Option<T>` represents an honest partial musical result: either `Some(value)` or `None`, with both cases handled explicitly.

```musa
let found: Option<Pitch> = None;
```

summary: a finite ordered collection type
doc:
`List<T>` is a finite ordered collection used by total folds and music-theory libraries. Square brackets construct its values.

```musa
let tones: List<Pitch> = [c4, e4, g4];
```

summary: a value, or the reason there is none
doc:
`Result<T, E>` is the binary sum, in the one shape this language has a use for: either `Ok(value)` or `Err(reason)`. Unlike `Option<T>` it says *which* way an operation failed, so an operation with two distinct failures returns one rather than asking the caller to re-derive the reason.

```musa
let series: Result<Row12, (List<Nat>, List<Pc12>)> = row12_of(sketch);
```

summary: handle every form of a finite value
doc:
A `match` expression names each possible case of an option, list, product, boolean, or other finite value. The checker requires complete, non-overlapping arms.

```musa
fn keep(x: Option<Pitch>) -> Option<Pitch> { match x { None -> None, Some(p) -> Some(p), } }
```

summary: choose between two values by a condition
doc:
`if condition { consequent } else { alternative }` is one expression, not a statement: it has a value, both branches have the same type, and the `else` is required. It is written out as the two-arm boolean `match` it stands for, so it costs exactly what that match costs.

```musa
fn clef_named(word: Text) -> Clef { if text_equal(word, "treble") { Treble } else { Bass } }
```

summary: the other branch of an `if`
doc:
`else` introduces the value an `if` takes when its condition is false. It is mandatory — a one-armed conditional would need a value for the case it does not cover, and this language has none. Writing another `if` after it makes a ladder.

```musa
if quarters(n) { Quarter } else if halves(n) { Half } else { Whole }
```

summary: an option containing a value
doc:
`Some(value)` constructs the present case of an `Option`; a `match` can bind the contained value. It carries its type's capital because it is one of that type's two constructors.

```musa
let tonic: Option<Pitch> = Some(c4);
```

summary: an option containing no value
doc:
`None` is the absent case of an `Option`. It makes partial musical operations explicit instead of hiding failure. `meter none;` is a different word: a meter that says there are no barlines.

```musa
let absent: Option<Pitch> = None;
```

summary: a result carrying the value that was wanted
doc:
`Ok(value)` constructs the left injection of `Result<T, E>`. It carries its type's capital because it is one of that type's two constructors.

```musa
let found: Result<Pitch, Text> = Ok(c4);
```

summary: a result carrying the reason there is no value
doc:
`Err(reason)` constructs the right injection of `Result<T, E>`. The reason is an ordinary value of the error type, not a second channel beside the returned one, so a `match` reads it the way it reads any other case.

```musa
let found: Result<Pitch, Text> = Err("no pitch spells that class here");
```

summary: the affirmative boolean value
doc:
`true` is one of the two `Bool` values and can be handled by `match`.

```musa
let enabled: Bool = true;
```

summary: the negative boolean value
doc:
`false` is one of the two `Bool` values and can be handled by `match`.

```musa
let muted: Bool = false;
```

summary: a collection rooted on a note
a scale ordinal, with no scale in it
doc:
A degree is a numbered position — 1 is the tonic, 8 the tonic a period higher — plus any chromatic alteration, and it belongs to no particular scale until one is supplied. Turning a degree into a note also needs a register, which is what a `Frame` carries. The word is reserved only so that the old spelling of the type gets one complaint carrying `Degree`.

```musa
let dominant: Degree = scale_degree(5);
```

summary: a scale that knows which octave
doc:
A frame is a scale plus the written pitch its first degree sounds, and it is the only thing that can turn a degree into a note. Building one fails unless the tonic pitch spells the scale's own tonic. The word is reserved only so that the old spelling of the type gets one complaint carrying `Frame`.

```musa
fn dominant_of(home: Frame) -> Pitch { frame_pitch(home, scale_degree(5)) }
```

summary: read this music in a scale
doc:
`in scale s { … }` supplies the pitch coordinates the enclosed music is read against, for `step` and for anything else that counts scale degrees. It is lexical and local: it emits no key signature and claims no modulation, so the same saved phrase can be used under two scales and mean two things.

```musa
in scale c dorian { use subject; }
```

summary: move by scale steps, not by an interval
doc:
`p step n` moves `n` degrees up the scale in force, and `p step down n` moves down; the answer depends on where in the scale `p` sits, which is exactly how `up M2` differs from it. The note stepped from has to be in the scale, and there has to be a scale.

```musa
in scale c major { (c5 step 2)/4 }
```

summary: rooted spelled content, with no register
doc:
`chord c major7` names a root and what is stacked on it, and nothing else: no octave, no spacing, no doubling, and no bass unless one is designated. It does not sound. Choosing the notes a player holds is a voicing policy, which can decline.

```musa
let harmony: chord_class = chord c major7;
```

summary: sound a chord in close position
doc:
`stack c4 major7/2` is sugar for the close-position voicing of that chord rooted at that written pitch, held for that long. The pitch is what fixes the register, so `stack c major7/2` is refused: a pitch class chooses no octave.

```musa
stack c4 major7/2
```

summary: parameterize a piece or a voice
name what a module must provide
group declarations behind a signature
declare a finite type of your own
doc:
A `data` declaration is a finite, strictly positive type with named constructors and named fields. It is how a package owns its own data instead of asking the compiler for another built-in type: the constructors are the only way in, `match` is how a reader takes one apart, and the generated fold — `motive_fold` for `data Motive` — is how a total traversal is written.

A field may not be a function, at any depth, and the declared type may not appear to the left of an arrow in its own group. Those two rules are what make the type finite and its fold terminating.

```musa
data Motive {
    Silence,
    Sounded(pitch: Pitch, held: Duration),
}
```

summary: the old spelling of `structure`
declare one child of a package's module tree
instantiate a template here
doc:
`make study(key g major) as study_in_g;` evaluates the arguments in the scope it is written in and expands the template into an ordinary declaration at this place. A piece instance stands at the file's root and is that file's piece; a voice instance stands among a part's voices. The `as` name is the address; identity comes from the site, so two instances with equal arguments remain two declarations.

```musa
make answer(subject, transpose(P8)) as follower;
```

summary: name what an instance makes
doc:
The mandatory second half of `make`. It is the source address other declarations refer to, and renaming it changes what can be written, not what the instance is.

```musa
make study(key g major) as study_in_g;
```
